rv.q: What’s most impressive about “Triumph” is how clear-eyed it is.
The concise running time, Churchill’s acerbic writing, and Ashford’s strong performance fully mining both the zany humor and scary relevance of the play make Triumph a rewarding if brief experience.
It certainly takes the "No Kings" movement to a heightened level of urgency.

Churchill’s central argument—that the enablement of authoritarianism throughout history has gotten us to where we are today—is undoubtedly important, but hardly revolutionary to an audience that’s already card-carrying members of the #Resistance.

Theater Caryl Churchill's 'Triumph' views imperial Rome through a Foxy blond flack (Off Broadway review) Date: October 18, 2026. Author: Thom Geier Time remains ever-bendable to human will. Just this week, Americans have invented an entirely new unit of time: a Zacharia, which is roughly half a Scaramucci.

cn.t: Critics praise Churchill's sharp, politically charged 20-minute play, which draws clever parallels between ancient Rome and contemporary politics through a press secretary's briefing, with Annaleigh Ashford's performance highlighting the veteran playwright's biting wit.

vr.q: Overall, this piece feels more like a sketch from a journal entry than anything else, or a political comic strip on stage.
I'm not really sure that this one worked for me.
